text: Everything up to this point has been setup. This lesson is where it pays off — writing the one SQL query that actually answers the Operations Manager's real question.

Back in Lesson 1, the vague ask became specific: show total units sold and total revenue by product category for August 2026. Every piece of that lives right in orders underscore raw — product category, quantity, and unit price. The query groups by category, sums quantity for total units, and sums quantity times unit price for total revenue.

One detail matters a lot here. Quantity times unit price has to be calculated per row, inside the sum, not after the fact. Summing quantity and summing unit price separately and then multiplying those two totals together is a completely different, wrong calculation. It's an easy mistake to make and an easy one to miss, because the wrong number still looks plausible.

Running this against the real data reveals something genuinely useful. Camp Kitchen sold the most units — eighteen hundred and forty-two of them. But Tents and Shelters earned the most revenue, over one hundred eighty-three thousand dollars, because tents cost far more per unit than a camp stove or a cooking pot. Two different, both valid, winners for sold the most.

This is exactly why the question got clarified back in Lesson 1. If the Operations Manager had only asked for units sold, the restock conversation would have completely missed the category actually driving the most revenue. Before trusting either number, it's worth spot-checking one category by hand against a few raw order rows — aggregation mistakes are invisible until you check for them.

The question is answered. Next lesson steps back and asks what would need to change about this setup if this same question got asked again and again, instead of just once — which is where partitioning earns its place.
